title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
description: Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.The overnig
body: Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity £1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity."But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over £11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another £7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

schema.headline: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips

title: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal
description: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBCFigure caption, Watch: Trailer for new programme detailing Princess Catherine
body: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBCFigure caption, Watch: Trailer for new programme detailing Princess Catherine's cancer journeyByRoyal correspondentThe Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC."It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day."It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William."It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.Image source, Matt Porteous/Kensington PalaceImage caption, Kensington Palace shared a photo of Catherine doing the Three Peaks Challenge, ahead of the documentaryCatherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy.In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, Catherine visited India for William's Earthshot Prize which was hosted in Mumbai - the first time she'd been at the Earthshot awards since 2022Among the film crew for the documentary, as director of photography, was Will Warr, who has worked with Catherine and her family before.His pictures have been used in a video birthday message by Catherine and a Christmas card which showed a relaxed image of the princess and Prince William and their children.The filmmaker also made the personal video statement that marked the end of her chemotherapy in September 2024, with her message: "Out of darkness, can come light."Kate Phillips, the BBC's chief content officer, said it was hoped the 30-minute documentary "will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges".Catherine was treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital and funds from the distribution of this documentary, which is to be broadcast in other countries, will be paid to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.When cancer patients finish treatment at the London hospital they can symbolically ring a bell."I didn't ring the bell," says Catherine, speaking to her brother James Middleton."Maybe this is your ringing the bell," he says, about carrying out the Three Peaks Challenge and this documentary about her healing.Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November. It will also air internationally, including on NBCUniversal in the US on 30 November, Channel 9 in Australia on 1 December and CTV and Noovo in Canada on 7 December

schema.headline: Princess of Wales: Catherine talks about her cancer journey in new documentary Heal

title: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes
description: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days l
body: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze."We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured"."So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

schema.headline: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes

title: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'
description: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he
body: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story"."It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm. "Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it."It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.Robins also hopes to raise the question - "do ghosts exist?", sparking the debate between belief and scepticism."What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy, who recently starred in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."Robins said The Witch Farm was "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in its creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from 22 November

schema.headline: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'

title: France 45-17 Argentina - Les Bleus secure final spot
description: Nations ChampionshipFrance (14) 45Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5Argentina (10) 17Tries: Picc
body: Nations ChampionshipFrance (14) 45Tries: Guillard, Mauvaka, Gourgues 2, Gailleton, Duguid, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Gourgues 5Argentina (10) 17Tries: Piccardo, Matera Cons: Albornoz 2 Pen: AlbornozFrance dispatched Argentina in Paris to book their spot against South Africa in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday.Knowing pre-game a bonus-point victory at Stade de France would be enough to edge England out of the top spot in the northern hemisphere standings, Les Bleus had to work hard to secure the points required.Lock Mickael Guillard powered over for the opening score, but Justo Piccardo responded for the visitors before Tomas Albornoz nudged them ahead with a penalty.Argentina have not been at their best this November, suffering a heavy defeat by Ireland before narrowly beating Italy.However, as is often the case with the Pumas, the longer they spend together, the more they tend to improve as a campaign progresses.Felipe Contepomi's side brought the first-half physicality needed to trouble France, who turned to their maul late in the first half to score through Peato Mauvaka and reclaim the lead.Fly-half Matthieu Jalibert, who missed the win over the world champions through injury, then expertly sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap to score.The pivotal moment came when Argentina prop Mayco Vivas was shown a 20-minute red card for making direct head contact at a ruck, with France capitalising on the extra man to score their bonus-point try through Emilien Gailleton.Hooker Julian Montoya then joined Vivas in the sin-bin after receiving a yellow card and France made their numerical advantage count once again as Tyler Duguid and Gourgues crossed.Pablo Matera intercepted Louis Bielle-Biarrey's pass to improve the scoreline but Bielle-Biarrey made amends to dot down a brilliant kick into space by Antoine Dupont.It will now be rematch of last Friday's epic game in Paris, which France narrowly won 21-19 against the world champions.South Africa booked their spot in the final by picking up a losing bonus point against Ireland.Scotland will play Argentina on Sunday at Allianz Stadium in the seventh/eighth-place play-off.France: Attissogbe; Grandidier-Nkanang, Gourgues, Moefana, Bielle-Biarrey; Jalibert, Dupont (capt); Jelonch, Ollivon, Capilla; Guillard, Verhaeghe; Falatea, Mauvaka, GrosReplacements: Lamothe, Poirot, Montagne, Duguid, Woki, Alldritt, Lucu, GailletonArgentina: Prisciantelli; Delguy, Cinti, Chocobares, Mendy; Albornoz, Benitez Cruz; Isa, Scelzo, Gonzalez; Lavanini, Petti; Moreno, Montoya (capt), WengerReplacements: Bosch, Vivas, Sclavi, Elias, Rubiolo, Matera, Moyano, IsgroSin bin: Vivas (61 mins), Montoya (67 mins)

title: Strait of Hormuz swim highlights environmental cost of war
description: Image source, Lewis Pugh FoundationImage caption, Pugh said the Strait of Hormuz has an "extraordinary natural world" beneath the surfaceByJake Wallac
body: Image source, Lewis Pugh FoundationImage caption, Pugh said the Strait of Hormuz has an "extraordinary natural world" beneath the surfaceByJake WallaceSouth WestA British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.Image source, Lewis Pugh FoundationImage caption, The Strait of Hormuz carries a significant share of global oil shipments from the Middle EastThe swimmer is believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in March.He swam from Musandam Island in the strait to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula.According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 4km (2.5 miles) from where he was swimming on the first day.On the second day, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from the burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier Tara Gas and later passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire."My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers on board," Pugh said."The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences - not just for crew members, but also on the surrounding marine environment."Image source, Lewis Pugh FoundationImage caption, Pugh has completed long-distance swims in every ocean of the worldPugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often receives less attention than the human cost."War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart, and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes," he said."But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped."The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.Pugh said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

schema.headline: Strait of Hormuz swim highlights environmental cost of war

title: Poppy Jay: An exhausting two days in the shoes of a British tradwife
description: Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.As a director and wri
body: Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife. On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life."I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress."What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."The tradwife phenomenon has been popularised on social media which has been a major driving force in its expansion.Some US creators have millions of followers - Hannah Neeleman, widely seen as one of the world's leading tradwife influencers, has 10.3 million users following her Instagram account, Ballerina Farm. However, another popular American influencer, Nara Smith, has rejected the label. Smith married young, has four children and her content centres on cooking food (or even making toothpaste) from scratch, but insists she's no tradwife."They kind of used me as the poster child of the tradwife movement, which was very bizarre to me," Smith said on the Call Her Daddy podcast. "Sure, do I love cooking... but that's a passion of mine, it's a hobby - it's not something that I need to be doing."The tradwife trend has also made its way into popular culture, with author Caro Claire Burke's satirical novel Yesteryear selling more than 1.4 million copies and Hollywood actress Anne Hathaway has signed up to produce and star in a film adaptation.Jay tells BBC News she saw how much work Molly did which had "parallels" with her upbringing in a conservative Muslim family, which included her entering an arranged marriage when she was 19. She and her husband divorced about five years later."I've helped raise my siblings, I know my way around a kitchen, I can cook, I tutored my siblings," Jay said. "Other than the chicken coop, it's not unfamiliar territory. But I think doing it for two days - I know this sounds ridiculous... it's just the relentless pace of her life."While Molly manages the house, her husband Aaron is a full-time theologian who shares his views on religion and anti-feminism on social media.When speaking to Jay, Aaron explained the reason the household work was down to his wife: "Molly's obviously omni-competent and brilliant but submission is still really hard," he says, "and when I say something that Molly disagrees with, that's when the submission really matters." While Molly says her social media does not make money, some tradwives do look to turn a profit through their posts.West Sussex couple Megan and Joseph Landreth-Smith have three children and have an Instagram account with nearly 6,000 followers.Megan often gets brand deals to share products on her Instagram, which she says helps with some extra income and "feels like a really natural fit" around what they are doing already - producing content while being with their children.Just like many influencers, trolls can be a problem, but they also help to bring in some money.With her husband Zion, Yorkshire-based life coach Laura Zachary promotes a course called the Academy of Biblical Wifery, based on their born-again Christian beliefs, to more than 32,000 Instagram followers."The more disagreement on a comments section, the more people that come to it and the more you get paid".The "appeal" which Jay identifies goes much broader - a report published by King's College London, external found 79% of women surveyed were drawn to the relaxed, calm lifestyle it portrays.But its co-author, Prof Heejung Chung, who specialises in researching the tradwife phenomenon, said that it can be the tip of a political change.The content might begin with "nice dresses", said Chung, but can "draw them towards more extremist, far-right, or nationalist ideologies, which ultimately seek to curtail women's autonomy and reinforce patriarchal authority".However, her report concludes most young women and men surveyed showed "largely progressive views on gender roles".For those who liked the content, it was down to its "lifestyle imagery", rather than "the traditional gender division of labour or power".But this does not mean the tradwife movement poses no risk to gender equality, the report says, and its "growing popularity... should not be dismissed or trivialised".

schema.headline: Poppy Jay: An exhausting two days in the shoes of a British tradwife

title: England 37-12 New Zealand: Can win over All Blacks finally break boom-bust cycle?
description: We have been here before of course.Twelve months ago, as today, England took a famous win over New Zealand.After a run of victories against lesser opp
body: We have been here before of course.Twelve months ago, as today, England took a famous win over New Zealand.After a run of victories against lesser opponents, it was the litmus test of their progress. They passed with flying colours and a comfortable scoreline.It was a statement victory, a sign of things to come. England were building into world-beaters.The similarities to today's 37-12 success are striking. Even the attendance figure - 81,953 - matches.For England fans, burned by the dismal Six Nations that followed the 2025 result, there will be a shot of caution with the celebratory drinks tonight.Steve Borthwick's four-year reign has been marked by booms and busts.Five defeats in six Tests preceded the 2023 Rugby World Cup, when they came within a point of making the final.They lost five straight matches in the back half of 2024, before embarking on 12-Test winning streak at the start of 2025.The sunny uplands have too often turned out to be false dawns.But, there are grounds to think this time, just maybe, is different.For a start, it is a different England team, playing a different way.When the team was named on Thursday, it was striking that England's backline contained none of the same starters as 12 months ago.Steward, Roebuck, Lawrence, Dingwall, Feyi-Waboso, Ford and Mitchell read the teamsheet for the 2025 win over New Zealand.Furbank, Murley, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph, Smith, and Van Poortvliet was its 2026 equivalent.But for injury, Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Alex Mitchell may have featured in both. Tommy Freeman likewise.But the balance has shifted.The class of 2026, with Fin Smith pulling strings, Henry Slade distributing to pace out wide, and George Furbank out the back and at first receiver, is a more fluid unit.Seb Atkinson, up against Jordie Barrett, was critical to England's variety, able to combine full-throated midfield carries with deft hands.In part, it is horses for courses.Twelve months ago, kicking and chasing was in vogue. And England were setting the trend.In their 2025 win over the All Blacks, England put boot to ball 35 times and passed it 104 times. A ratio of one to three.This time around, the stat showed 29 kicks to 176 passes. The boot is being used half as much in relative terms.The change has been forced to a degree. After a law tweak initially made the aerial route profitable last year, defences have found ways to counter, with retreating catchers and pockets of players posted to pick up scraps.England had to find new dimensions. And they have.Jack van Poortvliet and Ollie Chessum's tries were created by clever movement and midfield breaks by Cadan Murley and Will Joseph respectively.From similar positions 12 months ago, England would have been tempted to take to the skies.The current way of playing is less predictable, and more sustainable as a long-term tactic to threaten the game's superpowers at the backend of next year's Rugby World Cup.The balance of power up front has tilted further in England's favour as well.New Zealand were without talismanic captain Ardie Savea and fellow forwards Luke Jacobsen and Shannon Frizell. But still, England's heavy traffic ram-raided through the heart of the visiting pack a startling number of times.Ben Earl particularly had a field day. The number eight has been a star performer throughout his team's fluctuating form and stamped his authority on this contest with a whopping 33 carries and 138 metres made.Ellis Genge, Greg Fisilau and George Martin were abrasive off the bench, cementing England's advantage.Defensively, England were tight.Twelve months ago, New Zealand leapt out into a 12-0 lead with two tries in the first 17 minutes. They never looked like piling on points in a similar quickfire way this time around.The visitors had only three line breaks compared to nine in 2025.The dominance was near total. The All Blacks were all out of answers.And England would have been out of sight sooner with a fewer errors in the first half."It was a very good performance and what's exciting is we left some points out there - I think we can be even better," Borthwick told BBC Radio 5 Live afterwards."No journey of a team is ever linear. There are always ups and downs that you work through. We continue to strive to improve."This is a team that has got enormous growth in it and I'm excited about the journey."If players keep the attitude they have to want to get better - and you can see that with the defence, because it was a brilliant defensive performance - when you have that level of commitment, what the players can achieve, I'm excited by the possibilities."England's fans have certainly bought in.Lewis Moody's appearance alongside the team for the haka, after presenting them their shirts the previous evening, was an invite to emotionally invest that was impossible to turn down.The manner in which England's players, in the seconds before kick-off, sought Moody out to embrace him spoke of a bond.The crowd responded to something special and real.The All Blacks, famed aura faded, were reduced to minor roles.Beaten last weekend by Wales, their long season is in severe danger of fizzling out.If so, it is understandable. They have been set the most brutal of schedules.In the aftermath of July's Nations Championship they have played nine Tests in less than three months. Four of those were away to South Africa, with the final meeting in the Greatest Rivalry series staged in Baltimore to add a few more air miles to their dizzying itinerary.Battle-hardened can turn to over-cooked quickly. And with Ruben Love, Quinn Tupaea, Caleb Clarke and Leroy Carter out, their backline is as patched up as their pack.After a superb start to his All Blacks reign, Dave Rennie would be forgiven for wanted to recuperate and regroup.As it is, his side will be back at Allianz Stadium for a rematch against England in the Nations Championship third-place play-off next Saturday.There are big Tests down the road for Borthwick's side. Ireland away in the opening round of the Six Nations in February looms large.But they are measuring up well, compared to their own high watermarks, as well as the rest of the Test game.

schema.headline: England 37-12 New Zealand: Can win over All Blacks finally break boom-bust cycle?

title: We were priced out of the market, so we bought a home with strangers
description: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangersImage source, Elizabeth WilcoxImage caption, The Pullman family, on the left, and the
body: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangersImage source, Elizabeth WilcoxImage caption, The Pullman family, on the left, and the Wilcox family, bought a home together soon after meeting ByDavid SilverbergBusiness reporterReporting fromTorontoWhen Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in."We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.'We've saved thousands'They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".Image source, Elizabeth WilcoxImage caption, Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get alongWhile there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosai says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.Gosai is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche"."I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don't know."Image source, Elizabeth WilcoxImage caption, The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver homeThree years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer."If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.'We have house meetings'Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements."It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.Image source, Sabrina BowmanImage caption, Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move."I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."Get in touchAre you looking to get onto the property ladder? Share your experience.

schema.headline: We were priced out of the market, so we bought a home with strangers

title: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa
description: After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get ba
body: After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get back to the levels they had reached when considered squarely among that group.Because they had got there before came the typically uncomplicated response from the side's head coach.The longer the 2023 World Cup receded into memory, however, fewer and fewer believed that his side still had within them the type of performance they produced to beat the Springboks 20-17 on Saturday. Undoubtedly Ireland's biggest win of recent years, having not beaten one of the three sides who started this weekend above them in the rankings since the summer of 2024, this was one of their most needed too.This Test had long been viewed as one of the crucial measuring sticks for Farrell's side building towards next autumn's World Cup - the last time they will face the back-to-back champions before boarding the plane to Australia. Having settled into a pattern where they could not beat the best, but almost always found a way past the rest, Ireland could not have headed down under with genuine belief of making history without first showing they were still capable of this level. "It's something that we've been looking forward to, to challenge ourselves and delivering when it matters against top-line sides," said Farrell."We knew that this fixture was coming, playing against the world's best by a stretch at this moment in time"It was a game that we we wanted to challenge ourselves and see how we went and, obviously fronting up and showing the character that we did, and coming out on the right side of the win is a big night for everyone who is Irish."For all that had gone on in the build-up, from explosive news conferences to coaching suspensions, from dismissed citing complaints to eye-catching positional switches, by the time of kick-off, it almost felt as if a reminder was needed that there was still a game to be played.Some two hours later, with the banned Rassie Erasmsus having watched on from a nearby hotel with only a host of virtual followers on a near-silent YouTube stream for company, his Springboks side had lost consecutive games for the first time in four years.If his comments this week were designed to illicit a response from his side after last week's loss to France, he did not get the desired reaction. Instead, it was Ireland who it seemed had appropriately fuelled the fire.Virtually scrummaged off the park in this fixture last year, prop Andrew Porter was among those who said that day had stuck with them in the months since.While the tables were not turned at scrum-time, rather than allow the set-piece to again become the dominant thread of the game, this time around Ireland weathered the storm and came out the other side.Their aerial work in particular was key, with Farrell typically highlighting Robert Baloucoune's efforts to regather possession before mentioning the winger's second double in as many weeks."We were very good at just getting on with it," added the head coach."It's not always going to go your way against the world's best, certainly at scrum-time, they're world-leading in that regard. We took everything in isolation and just kept going on to the next moment."That was the story of the game, really."Even if South Africa had wrestled the game back in those frantic closing moments, this would not have been a loss to catalogue alongside the others against South Africa, France and New Zealand in recent years.Having started 2026 with their intent questioned after defeat in Paris, Ireland played their last home game of the year showing an appreciation that in these sorts of contests, it is the small moments that make for big results. A first-half scrum penalty of their own was greeted as raucously as a score while, whether it be a Joe McCarthy maul turnover, Mack Hansen's try-saving tackle on Canan Moodie or Hugo Keenan eating up the ground to thwart Kurt-Lee Arendse, Ireland continued to show that this time they were to stay in the fight. There will still be talk of whether this was truly Ireland absorbing South Africa's best punch - with both the Boks and All Blacks having lost twice in succession, questions will be asked of how much the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series has taken out of both sides. "We're not playing to our best potential," said captain Siya Kolisi."We know as a group we have better. I don't question the effort or the mindset, but it's executing better."Still, Ireland must believe that this was a game that said more about themselves than their opponents.

schema.headline: Nations Championship: Ireland remind themselves that the best are beatable with 20-17 win over South Africa

title: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
description: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of p
body: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.""Purebreds," says the woman filming.Warning: This story contains images some might find upsettingIn the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page."I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged."The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message."When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals.  "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila."So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths."Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.Or not, as the case may be.Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated."Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago."I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace."Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment."Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak"."I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says. "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN."Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said."To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more."We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.  "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

schema.headline: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

title: Chelsea 1-4 Leeds: Xabi Alonso's honeymoon period appears to be over
description: 'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is overFigure caption, Leeds dominate Chelsea for first Stamford Bridge win since 1999ByFoot
body: 'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is overFigure caption, Leeds dominate Chelsea for first Stamford Bridge win since 1999ByFootball reporter at Stamford BridgeChelsea manager Xabi Alonso is already in firefighting mode.His team were booed by their own supporters at several points during a dominant 4-1 Leeds victory at Stamford Bridge, their first win there since 1999.The first negative reaction came at half-time while the score was still 1-1. The ground then began to empty after the third and fourth Leeds goals, and the fans remaining voiced their dissent once more at the final whistle.Although there were mitigating circumstances, including a potentially harsh penalty decision against them and the loss of midfielder Moises Caicedo to injury, joining a five-strong list of players on the treatment table, the defeat was thoroughly deserved.It leaves Chelsea with three losses in their past four Premier League matches and they have slipped from fifth place to eighth, already 14 points behind league leaders Arsenal.In October, Tottenham won at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the Premier League era, while the 1-0 defeat at bottom club Sunderland before the international break was another alarm bell.It is the first time in 67 years that Chelsea have lost at home to both Leeds and Spurs in the same season. "We need to find solutions, for sure, because there will be setbacks during any game," Alonso said after the match."To be able to go through that and to know that it's still so long to play, it's something mandatory in this competition and today I felt that probably we are in a fragile moment mentally."When we received a punch we didn't recover that strongly."Indeed, even when Chelsea have been winning matches, they have often looked unconvincing.Yet Blues supporters chanted their new manager's name and seemed optimistic after the summer transfer business - despite a disappointing 10th-place finish last season. Club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers was joined by the experienced trio of Emiliano Martinez, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson.It was the clinical finishing of Rogers, along with Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro earlier in the season, that masked the underlying fragility of Alonso's team.Before this weekend, the Blues ranked 14th for expected goal difference and were joint 12th in Opta's expected points table.After their latest setback, ex-England forward and BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer said: "Chelsea were all over the place. Once Moises Caicedo went off injured early on, there was no physicality and they looked weak. "They hardly created anything going forward and the back four didn't look comfortable. There was no desire, cohesion or fight from the home side, but we shouldn't take anything away from Leeds. "Two weeks ago Chelsea were bullied by Sunderland centre-forward Brian Brobbey and they let Dominic Calvert-Lewin do the same today, which is alarming."It's fair to say Xabi Alonso's honeymoon period is over. He needs to tell his players this simply isn't good enough. They are miles off it and have to do better in every department."Figure caption, Xabi Alonso post-match interview - Chelsea v Leeds UnitedSo what's going wrong?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Xabi Alonso was appointed Chelsea manager on a four-year deal in MayIn Alonso's defence, Chelsea had problems before his arrival.They finished 10th last season, having been outrun in 37 of their 38 matches, and had three managers during a chaotic campaign.Remarkably, Chelsea have seven more points from corresponding fixtures this season and last, but it mostly serves to show how low the bar was set.Champions League qualification was again the club's pre-season target and Alonso's appointment was designed to bring stability and authority. The former Real Madrid and Liverpool midfielder had an impressive playing career and earned much early admiration as a manager, guiding Bayer Leverkusen to a league and cup double in 2024.However, the Spaniard, who was sacked by Real Madrid last season, has yet to establish any real consistency - beyond his defence leaking goals regularly.Only Crystal Palace, Coventry City and Ipswich Town have conceded more goals than Chelsea this season.Chelsea are also now averaging fewer than a goal per game since Joao Pedro suffered a thigh injury in training. Alongside Pedro and now Caicedo, Jorrel Hato, Maxence Lacroix, Reece James and Jamie Gittens are also injured.It highlights how they have gained little benefit of having a season without European football. Alonso is also beginning to face criticism from sections of the fanbase for both his team selections and substitutions.Chief among the reasons is the constant chopping and changing of the starting XI, having now made 28 line-up changes (behind only Tottenham) while also switching between back-four and back-three systems. In addition, Alonso is being criticised for his use of personnel, having deployed Pedro Neto as a striker on two occasions and, some would argue, not made enough use of exciting young winger Estevao.Figure caption, Chelsea have shown 'no progression' under Alonso - ShearerUncharted territory for AlonsoAgainst Leeds he gave striker Emmanuel Emegha his first start alongside Estevao and, although the Dutch striker scored, the pair were the first players he substituted while Chelsea were chasing the game at 3-1 down.Similarly, his late in-game interventions are under scrutiny, including the decision to bring on striker Welbeck only in the 90th minute of the defeat by Spurs.He took until the 64th minute to make changes against Leeds when Chelsea were already 3-1 down. Only three clubs had made more substitutions in the last 15 minutes than Chelsea in the league this season. Given Leeds' strengths, Chelsea should have been better prepared for what was coming. Before kick-off, Leeds had applied more high-intensity pressures in the opposition half than any other team in the Premier League.They had also generated the most expected goals from set-pieces and won the most duels. Leeds maintained those trends at Stamford Bridge against a Chelsea side often accused of being soft.Chelsea have had problems in recent seasons, but this was still their worst home defeat since a 4-1 loss to Brentford in 2022.Likewise, it is almost uncharted territory in Alonso's managerial career, having only previously lost at home by a three-goal margin once.The stadium emptied and supporters again left early.Players displayed negative body language and argued with one another both during the match and after the final whistle. As a result, Alonso has gone from needing to fix defensive issues to dealing with problems that appear to be spreading throughout the squad.Figure caption, 'Disgusting performance' - Chelsea fan furious after Leeds defeat

schema.headline: Chelsea 1-4 Leeds: Xabi Alonso's honeymoon period appears to be over

title: I've only sold five copies of GTA 6, says Leicester shop owner
description: Image caption, Richard Tewksbury said he had only sold five copies of GTA 6ByAdy DaymanBBC Radio Leicester and Will JeffordEast MidlandsThe owner of a
body: Image caption, Richard Tewksbury said he had only sold five copies of GTA 6ByAdy DaymanBBC Radio Leicester and Will JeffordEast MidlandsThe owner of an independent game shop says he has only sold five copies of the highly anticipated open-world action-adventure Grand Theft Auto 6.GTA 6, as it is known, is estimated to become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.But Richard Tewksbury, who runs Super Game Shack in the Silver Arcade in Leicester, said he had seen "embarrassing" sales of the game because it was only released as a digital download and not on disc."People are super, super, super hungry for this game - so it's already doing crazy numbers already - but that's not translated for us," he said."I've only sold four copies on PS5 and one copy on Xbox," added Tewksbury."It's because it's all digital - no-one sadly wants to buy a code in a box. We gave it a little go, but they just knocked it dead with making it digital. For game shops, it's a write-off."I'm really behind the game - I think it's amazing - but for shops, it's just not great."In June, developer Rockstar Games said physical copies would contain a code for a digital download rather than the more traditional format. The company has been contacted for comment.Tewksbury said, while he thinks the game is "amazing", the choice to not sell physical copies with discs was "not great" for smaller stores. The release of the blockbuster came after two delays to its initial launch date in autumn 2025.In advance of the launch, GTA 6 generated an estimated £1.25bn ($1.65bn) in revenue based on an estimated 17.07 million units sold, sales tracker SensorTower said, external.  However, Tewksbury said sales at local stores had been poor because physical editions contained download codes rather than discs."It is possibly the biggest game hype there's ever been - 13 years people have been waiting for this," he said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, GTA 6 generated an estimated £1.25bn ($1.65bn) in revenue based on pre-salesGTA 6 is one of the first major games to only be released without a traditional disc version.However, Tewksbury said the reality for game shops was that this style of release would be the future of the industry. Many consoles are now without physical disc drives and PlayStation announced in July that its games would no longer be released on discs from January 2028.Sony, which owns PlayStation, said the move came "as consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital"."This is the way it's going to be," Tewksbury said. "It's a big effect for us because it was such a massive game - everyone wants it. "A lot of people aren't even aware that you could actually get it as a code in a box in a shop."Suddenly everyone's already pre-ordered it months in advance because the download is so large and [they] aren't thinking about us."There was frustration from many gamers when it was announced that there would be no disc copies of GTA 6.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, GTA 6 was released on Thursday after a 13-year waitRob Spence, physical media collector and TikToker, said there was "outrage" over more games being released without a disc. "There're so many great benefits to physical media," he told BBC Radio Leicester."For me personally, it's that ability to touch, to hold, to really admire the artwork that goes into the casing and how it's all put together. "I always think there's nothing better than walking into a room and seeing a library or a shelf full of great pieces in a collection that can't ever be taken away from you. "There are so many great retailers out there, like the shop in Leicester, people should go and support them."Nothing beats holding the game." Image source, Rob SpenceImage caption, Rob Spence said the gaming community could lose its "sense of belonging"Spence, from Rothley in Leicestershire, said town and cities might see "another wave" of closures, if stores did not find ways of further diversifying as sales of physical games decreased."It's a very sad thought and unfortunately, this is just the first wave of these types of releases," he said. "We are now going to see more of this in 2027, and then we're going to see a lot more of it in 2028."He added the gaming community could lose its "sense of belonging" that came with the stores. "We all remember that community feel these shops should have, whether you came in at 10am on a Saturday with your pocket money to buy a latest release - we're going to miss all that," he said."But we're also now going to miss the midnight releases, when again, there was that sense of community, that sense of belonging."That sort of party atmosphere to be one of the first to get your hands on a game - that will all go."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Leicester

schema.headline: I've only sold five copies of GTA 6, says Leicester shop owner

title: Suffolk village votes to 'leave UK' over RAF Barnham migrant plan
description: Image source, Henry Godfrey-Evans/BBCImage caption, Helen Beck, chair of Barnham Residents' Association, with the village's new flagByGeorge KingSuffo
body: Image source, Henry Godfrey-Evans/BBCImage caption, Helen Beck, chair of Barnham Residents' Association, with the village's new flagByGeorge KingSuffolkVillagers vowed "this is only the beginning" after voting overwhelmingly to "leave the UK" in protest at plans to house migrants at a former airbase.Residents in Barnham, Suffolk, held a symbolic poll on Saturday to decide whether or not to declare independence.The referendum was called after RAF Barnham, near Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk and Thetford, in Norfolk, was earmarked by the government as a site to house up to 931 male asylum seekers.Two-hundred-and-fifty-seven people - 94% of those who took part – voted in favour of leaving, 16 voted against and one vote was spoiled.Following the result, which is not legally binding, residents unveiled a flag - a Stone-curlew against a Suffolk blue background - to celebrate the village's newfound "independence".Barnham is the second village to hold a symbolic poll over migrant housing plans, after residents of Piddington in Oxfordshire voted to leave the UK in September.John Bauer, chair of the parish council, has said the Suffolk village will now declare itself the Bailiwick of Barnham.Image source, Henry Godfrey-Evans/BBCImage caption, The voting took place at Barnham Village Hall, as journalists gathered outsideHelen Beck, chair of Barnham Residents' Association, was delighted with both the outcome and the conduct of all involved."I'm really very, very pleased, but also pleased the residents who didn't agree [with leaving] felt able to come and vote accordingly," she said."I would hate to think we weren't prepared to listen to all voices. "The community has come together around this, and I'm really, really grateful for everybody's support."Image source, Henry Godfrey-Evans/BBCImage caption, Ken Jordan said winning the result had given residents a huge boost to campaign even harder against the plansCampaigner Ken Jordan said the vote marked "just the beginning and the real work starts tomorrow".He added: "It's raised the profile, and it's given us a starting block now to launch the more serious side of our campaign."The government first put forward plans to house "single adult male" asylum seekers at RAF Barnham back in June.The proposals triggered demonstrations outside the former base. It is part of the government's drive to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers – a scheme which, at its peak, was reportedly costing £9m per day.Image source, Henry Godfrey-Evans/BBCImage caption, Pat Webb told the BBC she would be scared to leave her home alone if migrants were moved into RAF BarnhamBarnham resident Pat Webb, 69, stressed that the village was "not racist" but claimed it would be "overrun" if asylum seekers were allowed to move onto the base."The women in this village are scared," she said."I've got a little dog I walk round the village, and I'm not going to be able to do that unless my husband comes with me because I won't dare be out on my own."We've had a lovely retirement here so far, and it's all going to change, and for the worse, which is such a shame."Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBCImage caption, Patricia Gilson has lived in Barnham for "20 odd years"Patricia Gilson also voted in favour of leaving the UK."I'm mainly concerned about all these young men with nothing to do," she said."My neighbours with kiddies are worried to death, but the government isn't listening, but you just have to keep battling."The independence vote attracted national and international media attention.Zia Yusuf, Reform UK's spokesperson for home affairs, who was in Barnham as the result was announced, said it "tells you everything you need to know about how disenfranchised many people are".Barnham's Labour MP Peter Prinsley said he was "not surprised"."I'm due to meet the immigration minister this week when I will express the opposition felt by people in Barnham. I'm still optimistic the decision will be that this is not a suitable place for asylum seekers," he added.Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBCImage caption, Stephanie Donaldson said the Home Office had not consulted with residents as much as it said it hadBarnham resident Stephanie Donaldson, 31, said the vote had been "to try to draw attention" to the strength of "discontent" in the village."We live directly opposite [RAF Barnham] and obviously there's welfare and safety concerns for our children," she said."I think if [the facility] was properly secure without [people] being able to wander, perhaps that would've been better."The government said a final decision had not yet been made, but if it did proceed the "safety and security" of the community would be "of the utmost importance".A Home Office spokesperson said: "We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised."Additional reporting by Henry Godfrey-Evans, Zoie O'Brien, Jamie Niblock, and Andrew Sinclair.Do you have a story suggestion for Suffolk? title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
description: The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European U
body: The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays. The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge. The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530. There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime."So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially. British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027. The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU. The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme. In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027". Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants? "Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

schema.headline: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
